summary: This informational report covers the IAB workshop held online on November 9-13, 2020 about network impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic, when quarantine and working from home changed Internet user behavior and traffic. Researchers, operators and network management experts shared experiences. It reports the proceedings and does not necessarily reflect IAB views.

eli5.summary: When everyone stayed home during the pandemic, internet use changed a lot. Experts met online to share what happened to networks, and this document is the notes from that meeting.

subtitle: How the pandemic changed Internet traffic and what it revealed about networks

tldr.problem: COVID-19 lockdowns in 2020 caused sudden, massive changes in Internet traffic: people moved from offices to homes, video conferencing spiked, and traffic patterns shifted from evening peaks to all-day use.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Architecture Board convened researchers and operators who shared measurement data from networks, clouds, ISPs, and mobile carriers to document what actually happened and how networks responded.
tldr.outcome: The Internet coped better than expected because operators had spare capacity and responded quickly. The crisis revealed gaps in network observability and showed that the Internet is resilient but needs better measurement, security coordination, and equitable access.

today: RFC 9075 is the workshop report, published in July 2021. It remains a unique contemporaneous account of how the Internet handled the largest sudden traffic shift in its history and what that revealed about resilience and observability.

sections.title: The Workshop and the Crisis
sections.content:
In November 2020, as COVID-19 lockdowns were ongoing, the Internet Architecture Board held a workshop to collect and discuss measurement data on how the pandemic affected Internet traffic. Forty-six participants from network operators, researchers, cloud providers, and government attended online. Fifteen position papers provided measurement data and field reports from around the world.

The workshop confirmed that traffic volume surged 15–20% in just weeks—a growth that would normally take a year. Yet the Internet remained largely stable. This report documents what the measurements showed about traffic changes, operational responses, network security impacts, and lessons for future resilience.
sections.eli5: Internet engineers and operators from around the world shared their data on what happened to networks when quarantine started, and this is their combined report.

sections.title: Traffic Surge and Application Shifts
sections.content:
Traffic at Internet Exchange Points (IXPs) and ISPs grew 15–20% in March–April 2020, with some IXPs seeing record annual growth in a single year. Critically, this growth moved outside peak hours: traffic flattened across the day and weekends, eliminating the evening peak that had historically driven network design.

Application mix changed dramatically. Video conferencing (Zoom, Microsoft Teams) traffic increased over 200%, VPN usage doubled, while entertainment streaming remained high. However, content delivery networks showed reduced growth, and gaming had mixed results. Mobile networks saw different patterns: as people stayed home, mobile traffic actually declined, offsetting the surge in residential broadband.
sections.eli5: Much more Internet use during the day, not just evening. Video calls exploded, but mobile networks got quieter because nobody was traveling.

sections.title: Operational Readiness and Adaptation
sections.content:
Most operators handled the surge quickly by activating reserve capacity and adding bandwidth. Diurnal congestion appeared briefly in March but resolved within weeks as capacity was added, particularly at major interconnection points. Last-mile connections showed more persistent stress: 55% of measured networks experienced temporary congestion, especially in Japan and densely populated areas.

Cloud platforms generally avoided persistent congestion, though regional download throughput to public clouds declined over time, likely from increased load. The Internet's design assumption of spare capacity—intentionally leaving room for traffic to shift—proved crucial. Networks that ran close to their limits struggled more than those with safety margins.
sections.eli5: Networks had some extra capacity waiting. When demand spiked, operators turned it on. But some last-mile connections got crowded for a while.

sections.title: Security Threats and Digital Divide
sections.content:
Malicious actors quickly adapted. Phishing and scams using COVID-19 as a lure spiked. VPN software became a target as more people used it for remote work. However, overall cybercrime levels did not increase dramatically; the shift was toward COVID-themed attacks. Security coordination through Indicators of Compromise (IoC) sharing was very effective, suggesting that collective defense works during crises.

The pandemic also exposed the digital divide: areas with lower incomes had slower download speeds. Some ISPs (Comcast, Cox) responded by increasing speeds for lower-cost plans in affected areas, suggesting capacity was available but not always provisioned equally. This raised questions about equitable access and whether crisis response can also improve fairness.
sections.eli5: Scammers used COVID-19 lures. People sharing information about attacks helped defenders respond quickly. But some areas had much slower Internet, showing that inequality matters.

sections.title: Lessons and Future Needs
sections.content:
The workshop drew five main conclusions. First, the Internet's resilience came from spare capacity and quick human coordination, not from algorithmic sophistication. Second, operators lack shared observability: each has their own view, but nobody sees the whole picture, making troubleshooting hard when problems cross network boundaries. Third, resilience requires running networks with safety margins, not squeezing them for peak efficiency. Fourth, collaboration between operators, cloud providers, and application developers was vital. Fifth, the Internet's generality—designed to support many applications and scenarios—allowed it to adapt.

Key recommendations include monitoring Internet health continuously, sharing security defenses (IoC), ensuring broadband access for all, improving collaboration between sectors, and investing in resilience over optimization.
sections.eli5: The Internet worked because: networks had spare capacity, people cooperated, and the design was flexible. To stay ready for the next crisis, we need better measurements, shared security information, fair access for everyone, and networks that are not squeezed too tight.
